analysis.one_liner: Lets patients sue health plans under state law when a denied claim causes injury or death.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up in committee and died at the end of the 111th Congress with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a federal law called ERISA, most people with employer-based health insurance can only recover the cost of the denied benefit when a plan wrongly refuses to pay for care — they cannot sue for the harm that followed, even injury or death. This bill would change that: it would carve out a right for patients (or their estates) to bring state-law lawsuits for personal injury or wrongful death against the health plan, the insurer, or a managed-care company when a medically questionable claim denial caused the harm. Employers who sponsor plans would mostly keep their shield from lawsuits unless they personally took part in the denial.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer-based health coverage who are seriously harmed when their plan denies a claim for care. Today, under ERISA's broad preemption of state law, the most they can usually recover is the value of the benefit itself, even if the denial led to disability or death [S2][S3]. The bill would let them pursue state-law damages from the plan, insurer, or managed-care entity behind a 'medically reviewable decision' — a denial of, delay in, or failure to act on a benefits claim [S3]. It protects doctors, other treating providers, and hospitals acting purely as caregivers from being swept into those suits [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients harmed by denied health claims

how_it_helps.text: Amends ERISA so federal preemption no longer blocks state-law causes of action for personal injury or wrongful death arising from a denial of benefits under a group health plan [S2][S3].
Allows suits against the plan, its sponsor, the health insurance issuer, or any managed care entity involved in deciding how care or reimbursement is provided [S2][S3].

Excludes treating physicians and treating hospitals from the new liability, and keeps employers and plan sponsors shielded from suits unless they directly participated in the denial decision itself [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed-care companies, which would face state-court lawsuits and damage awards for denied or delayed claims, plus employers with self-funded plans in the narrow case where they directly made or controlled the denial decision [S2][S3]. Higher litigation risk and damage awards could also push up premiums and plan costs broadly.

drawbacks.text: Opening plans to jury damages for claim denials would raise insurers' litigation costs and settlement exposure, which could translate into higher premiums for all covered workers [S2][S3].
Liability could encourage defensive medicine — more tests, referrals, and paperwork to avoid denial-based suits — adding to health care spending.

Employers and plan sponsors would keep near-total immunity from state-law suits unless they directly made or controlled a particular denial, so the worst plan-design practices — low caps, high copays, narrow networks — would remain outside the reach of the courts [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real gap: a worker whose plan wrongly denies life-sustaining care today generally cannot recover more than the cost of the care itself. Giving patients state-law remedies is a genuine deterrent against claim denials. The main costs are higher litigation expense and premium pressure, and the design choices — shielding employers for ordinary plan decisions, excluding treating providers — are reasonable ways to limit the exposure. On balance the benefit to injured patients outweighs the cost, though the bill died without any refinement or debate, so its practical effects were never tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott (D-WA) introduced the bill on October 26, 2009 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S5].
On December 8, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No markup, report, or floor vote ever occurred; the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed-care companies keep the ERISA shield that limits their liability for denied claims to the cost of the benefit itself, sparing them state-court damages suits; injured patients remain unable to sue for the harm caused by a denial.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers keep their ERISA liability shield

for.name: Rep. Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Education and Labor Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. George Miller, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, sent it to its Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee, and never took it up for a markup or reported it.

sides.party_line_note: A single House Democrat sponsored the bill, it drew no cosponsors from either party, and the Democratic-led committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would let patients sue them under state law for injury or death caused by a denied or delayed claim, instead of being limited to recovering only the cost of the benefit. ERISA preemption is a major legal protection the industry has relied on since the 1970s, so preserving it is worth a great deal to insurers and a denial's victims alike.

Employers would keep their near-total shield from state-law suits for plan design decisions like copays and coverage limits, but would face suits when they directly made or controlled a claim denial. Keeping the shield keeps plan litigation costs off employers, but it also leaves employees without recourse for the design choices behind a denial.

The bill explicitly excludes treating doctors, other treating providers, and hospitals acting solely as caregivers from the new liability, so they gain the deterrent against wrongful denials without added malpractice-style exposure.
